title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 892–894 (Night 215, continuing nights-214), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 215 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Left behind in the orchard, he rents it from its owner, packs the rest of the gold in fifty more jars under olives, and learns that the ship sails only once a year; he weeps night and day over the loss of Budūr's stone. The ship meanwhile reaches the Ebony Isle, where Budūr, reigning there as king, sees it from her window and rides down to the shore. The captain lists his cargo, and at the mention of ʿAṣāfīrī olives she buys the fifty jars of the absent merchant for a thousand dirhams. That night, alone with Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, she tips out a jar and finds it full of red gold; in the gold she finds the stone that was tied to her drawstring, the one Qamar al-Zamān took, and she cries out for joy and falls in a swoon; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifteenth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and fifteenth night,
sentences.n: al-khāmisata ʿashara, “fifteenth”: as in the nights before, the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا سَافَرَتِ الْمَرْكَبُ رَجَعَ إِلَى ذٰلِكَ الْبُسْتَانِ وَجَلَسَ مَهْمُومًا مَغْمُومًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā sāfarati al-markabu rajaʿa ilā dhālika al-bustāni wa-jalasa mahmūman maghmūman
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when (she) sailed, the-ship, returned to that garden and-sat anxious, grieved.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the ship had sailed, Qamar al-Zamān went back to that garden and sat there, careworn and sorrowful.
sentences.n: Qamara is accusative after anna. lammā sāfarati al-markabu, “when the ship sailed”: the verb is feminine, though markab is masculine; the print goes on treating the ship as feminine, as the spoken language often does. mahmūman maghmūman, “anxious, grieved”, the rhyming pair of the night before, tell how he sat.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَأْجَرَهُ مِنْ صَاحِبِهِ وَأَقَامَ تَحْتَ يَدِهِ رَجُلًا يُعَاوِنُهُ عَلَى سَقْيِ الشَّجَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-istaʾjarahu min ṣāḥibihi wa-aqāma taḥta yadihi rajulan yuʿāwinuhu ʿalā saqyi al-shajari
sentences.l: And-he-rented-it from its-owner, and-set-up under his-hand a-man helping-him in watering the-trees.
sentences.i: He rented it from its owner, and took on a man under him to help him water the trees.
sentences.n: The print has واستاجرة, a misprint for واستاجره, corrected here. istaʾjara, Form X of ajara, “to hire, rent”: -hu is the garden, and min marks the one it is rented from, its ṣāḥib, “owner”, now that the old gardener who kept it is dead. aqāma, Form IV, “to set up, appoint”. taḥta yadihi, “under his hand”, that is, in his service. yuʿāwinuhu, Form III, “helping him”, describes the man; ʿalā marks the task helped with. saqy, “watering”; al-shajar, “the trees”, a collective.

sentences.t: وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الطَّابَقِ وَنَزَلَ إِلَى الْقَاعَةِ وَعَبَّى الذَّهَبَ الْبَاقِيَ فِي خَمْسِينَ مَطَرًا وَرَمَى فَوْقَهُ الزَّيْتُونَ
sentences.tr: wa-tawajjaha ilā al-ṭābaqi wa-nazala ilā al-qāʿati wa-ʿabbā al-dhahaba al-bāqiya fī khamsīna maṭaran wa-ramā fawqahu al-zaytūna
sentences.l: And-he-went to the-trapdoor and-went-down to the-hall, and-packed the-gold the-remaining in fifty jars, and-threw over-it the-olives.
sentences.i: Then he went to the trapdoor, went down into the hall, and packed the rest of the gold into fifty jars, throwing olives over it.
sentences.n: al-ṭābaq, “the trapdoor”, and al-qāʿa, “the hall”, are the rock-cut treasure chamber of the night before. al-dhahab al-bāqī, “the remaining gold”: the gardener's half, which is now his. ʿabbā, Form II, “to fill, pack (a vessel)”, a word of the later language, spelt with ى. maṭar, “jar”, the singular accusative after khamsīn, “fifty”. ramā fawqahu, “he threw over it”: -hu is the gold.

sentences.t: وَسَأَلَ عَنِ الْمَرْكَبِ فَقَالُوا لَهُ إِنَّهَا لَا تُسَافِرُ إِلَّا فِي كُلِّ سَنَةٍ مَرَّةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: wa-saʾala ʿani al-markabi fa-qālū lahu innahā lā tusāfiru illā fī kulli sanatin marratan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: And-he-asked about the-ship, and-they-said to-him: Indeed-it not sails except in every year one time.
sentences.i: He asked about the ship, and they told him that it sailed only once a year.
sentences.n: saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿan marks what is asked after; the hamza of وسأل is printed. “They” are left unnamed, the people of the town. innahā after qāla brings in their words; -hā is the ship, feminine again. lā … illā, “not … except”, that is, “only”. marratan wāḥidatan, “one time”, an accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَزَادَ بِهِ الْوَسْوَاسُ وَتَحَسَّرَ عَلَى مَا جَرَى لَهُ لَاسِيَّمَا فَقْدُ الْفَصِّ الَّذِي هُوَ لِلسِّتِّ بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: fa-zāda bihi al-waswāsu wa-taḥassara ʿalā mā jarā lahu lā siyyamā faqdu al-faṣṣi alladhī huwa li-al-Sitti Budūra
sentences.l: And-grew-greater in-him the-anxious-whispering, and-he-sighed-in-regret over what had-befallen him, especially (the) loss (of) the-stone which it (was) for-the-Lady Budūr.
sentences.i: His troubled thoughts grew upon him, and he grieved over all that had befallen him, above all the loss of the stone that belonged to the Lady Budūr.
sentences.n: zāda bihi, “it increased in him”: bi- marks the one it weighs on. waswās, “whispering”, the inner voice of anxiety and dark thoughts (also the whisper of the Devil). taḥassara ʿalā, Form V, “to sigh with regret over”: ʿalā marks what is regretted; its shadda is printed. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it befalls. The print sets lā siyyamā, “especially”, solid as لاسيما, kept so; the noun after it may take any case, and it is read here as nominative, faqdu. faqd, “loss”, a verbal noun. alladhī huwa li-, “which is for”, that is, “which belongs to”: li- marks the owner. al-Sitt, “the Lady”, the later language's title for a woman of rank.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ يَبْكِي بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ وَيُنْشِدُ الْأَشْعَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra yabkī bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri wa-yunshidu al-ashʿāra
sentences.l: And-he-began weeping by-the-night and-the-day, and-reciting the-verses.
sentences.i: And he took to weeping night and day and reciting verses.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he came to do”, that is, “he began to”. bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri, “by night and day”: bi- marks the time. ashʿār, plural of shiʿr, “poetry, verses”. The rhyme falls on al-nahār / al-ashʿār; no verses follow in the print.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَرْكَبِ فَإِنَّهَا طَابَ لَهَا الرِّيحُ وَوَصَلَتْ إِلَى جَزِيرَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri Qamari al-Zamāni wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-markabi fa-innahā ṭāba lahā al-rīḥu wa-waṣalat ilā Jazīrati al-Ābanūsi
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) Qamar al-Zamān. And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) the-ship, then-indeed-it — was-good for-it the-wind, and-it-arrived at (the) Isle (of) the-Ebony.
sentences.i: So much for Qamar al-Zamān. As for the ship, the wind was fair for her, and she came to the Ebony Isle.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amri …, wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what happened with … ; and as for what happened with …”: the storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the tale and taking up another. ammā … fa-, “as for … then”: the fa- that answers ammā here falls on inna; the shadda of فانّها is printed. ṭāba lahā al-rīḥu, “the wind was good for her”: li- marks whom the fair wind serves, and ṭāba is masculine with rīḥ, as in the night before. The madda of الآبنوس is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ بِالْأَمْرِ الْمُقَدَّرِ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ كَانَتْ جَالِسَةً فِى الشُّبَّاكِ الْمُطِلِّ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna bi-al-amri al-muqaddari anna al-malikata Budūra kānat jālisatan fī al-shubbāki al-muṭilli ʿalā al-baḥri
sentences.l: And-it-was by-the-matter the-foreordained that the-queen Budūr was sitting in the-window the-overlooking upon the-sea.
sentences.i: And as fate had decreed, Queen Budūr was sitting at the window that looked out over the sea.
sentences.n: kāna bi-al-amri al-muqaddari anna …, “it was by the decreed matter that …”: bi- marks the cause, and the anna clause is the subject of kāna. muqaddar, Form II passive participle, “decreed, foreordained”; its shadda is printed. al-malika, “the queen”: the narrator calls Budūr queen, though in the Ebony Isle she reigns disguised as a man and is addressed as king. shubbāk, “window”, often a latticed one; فى is spelt with ى. al-muṭill ʿalā, Form IV participle of aṭalla, “overlooking”: ʿalā marks what lies below; the shadda of المطلّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَقَدْ أَرْسَتْ فِى السَّاحِلِ فَخَفَقَ فُؤَادُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilā al-markabi wa-qad arsat fī al-sāḥili fa-khafaqa fuʾāduhā
sentences.l: And-she-looked at the-ship, and-it-had already anchored at the-shore, and-throbbed her-heart.
sentences.i: She looked at the ship as it lay at anchor by the shore, and her heart beat fast.
sentences.n: naẓara ilā, “to look at”: ilā marks what is looked at. wa-qad arsat, “it having anchored”, a circumstantial clause: arsā, Form IV of rasā, “to cast anchor, come to rest”; the ship is feminine once more. sāḥil, “shore”; فى is spelt with ى. khafaqa, “to throb, flutter”; fuʾād, “heart”, and its ؤ is printed.

sentences.t: وَرَكِبَتْ هِيَ وَالْأُمَرَاءُ وَالْحُجَّابُ وَالنُّوَّابُ وَجَاءَتْ إِلَى السَّاحِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-rakibat hiya wa-al-umarāʾu wa-al-ḥujjābu wa-al-nuwwābu wa-jāʾat ilā al-sāḥili
sentences.l: And-she-mounted, she and-the-emirs and-the-chamberlains and-the-deputies, and-she-came to the-shore.
sentences.i: She rode out with the emirs, the chamberlains and the deputies, and came down to the shore.
sentences.n: rakibat hiya wa-…, “she rode, she and …”: the verb stays singular and feminine, and hiya is spelt out so that the others can be joined to the subject. umarāʾ, plural of amīr, “emir, commander”. ḥujjāb, plural of ḥājib, “chamberlain”, the officer who guards the ruler's door; its shadda is printed. nuwwāb, plural of nāʾib, “deputy, lieutenant”; the shadda on the nūn of والنّواب is printed.

sentences.t: وَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَقَدْ دَارَ الشَّيْلُ وَالنَّقْلُ فِي الْبَضَائِعِ إِلَى الْمَخَازِنِ
sentences.tr: wa-waqafat ʿalā al-markabi wa-qad dāra al-shaylu wa-al-naqlu fī al-baḍāʾiʿi ilā al-makhāzini
sentences.l: And-she-stood by the-ship, and-had already gone-round the-lifting and-the-carrying in the-goods to the-storehouses.
sentences.i: She stood by the ship, where the lifting and carrying of the goods to the storehouses was already under way.
sentences.n: waqafa ʿalā, “to stand over, by”: ʿalā marks what one stands at. wa-qad dāra …, a circumstantial clause: dāra, “to go round”, here “to get going, be in full swing”. shayl, “lifting, carrying”, is the verbal noun of the later language's shāla, “to lift”; naql, “carrying, transport”. fī al-baḍāʾiʿi: fī marks what the work is busy with, the goods; baḍāʾiʿ, plural of biḍāʿa, “merchandise”, and its ئ is printed. makhāzin, plural of makhzan, “storehouse”.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرَتِ الرَّئِيسَ وَسَأَلَتْهُ عَمَّا مَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍarati al-raʾīsa wa-saʾalathu ʿammā maʿahu
sentences.l: And-she-had-brought the-captain and-asked-him about-what (was) with-him.
sentences.i: She had the captain brought before her and asked him what he carried.
sentences.n: aḥḍara, Form IV, “to have (someone) brought, summon”. al-raʾīs, “the captain”, and its ئ is printed, as is the hamza of وسألته. ʿammā is ʿan + mā, “about what”: ʿan marks what is asked about. maʿahu, “with him”, his cargo.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ مَعِي فِي هٰذِهِ الْمَرْكَبِ مِنَ الْعَقَاقِيرِ وَالْأَكْحَالِ وَالسُّفُوفَاتِ وَالْأَدْهَانِ وَالْمَرَاهِمِ وَالْأَمْوَالِ وَالْبَضَائِعِ النَّفِيسَةِ وَالْأَقْمِشَةِ الْفَاخِرَةِ وَالْأَنْطَاعِ الْيَمَانِيَّةِ مَا يَعْجِزُ عَنْ حَمْلِهِ الْجِمَالُ وَالْبِغَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ayyuhā al-maliku maʿī fī hādhihi al-markabi mina al-ʿaqāqīri wa-al-akḥāli wa-al-sufūfāti wa-al-adhāni wa-al-marāhimi wa-al-amwāli wa-al-baḍāʾiʿi al-nafīsati wa-al-aqmishati al-fākhirati wa-al-anṭāʿi al-yamāniyyati mā yaʿjizu ʿan ḥamlihi al-jimālu wa-al-bighālu
sentences.l: And-he-said: O king, with-me in this ship (is), of the-drugs and-the-eye-powders and-the-powders and-the-oils and-the-ointments and-the-wealth and-the-goods the-precious and-the-stuffs the-splendid and-the-leathers the-Yemeni, what are-unable to carry-it the-camels and-the-mules.
sentences.i: He said, “O king, I have in this ship drugs and kohls, powders, oils and ointments, wealth and precious goods, splendid stuffs and Yemeni leathers, more than camels and mules could carry.
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here. The captain addresses Budūr as ayyuhā al-maliku, “O king”, for so she is known in the island. hādhihi al-markab, “this ship”, feminine again. maʿī, “with me (is)”, is the predicate, and its subject is mā, “what”, held back to the end; the long list comes before it, brought in by min, “of”, which marks the kinds that mā sums up: “of drugs … what the camels cannot carry”. ʿaqāqīr, plural of ʿaqqār, “drug, medicinal herb”. akḥāl, plural of kuḥl, “kohl, eye-powder”. sufūfāt, plural of safūf, “a medicine taken dry as a powder”. adhān, plural of duhn, “oil, unguent”; marāhim, plural of marham, “ointment”. aqmisha, plural of qumāsh, “cloth, stuff”. anṭāʿ, plural of niṭʿ, “a mat or spread of leather”; yamānī, “of Yemen”, a by-form of yamanī. ʿajaza ʿan, “to be unable to”: ʿan marks what is beyond one. The verb is singular before its plural subjects, al-jimāl, “camels”, and al-bighāl, “mules”.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ أَصْنَافِ الْعِطْرِ وَالْبَهَارِ وَمِنَ الْعُودِ الْقَاقُلِّيِّ وَالتَّمْرِ الْهِنْدِيِّ وَالزَّيْتُونِ الْعَصَافِيرِيِّ مَا يَنْدُرُ وُجُودُهُ فِي هٰذِهِ الْبِلَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-min aṣnāfi al-ʿiṭri wa-al-bahāri wa-mina al-ʿūdi al-qāqulliyyi wa-al-tamri al-hindiyyi wa-al-zaytūni al-ʿaṣāfīriyyi mā yandaru wujūduhu fī hādhihi al-bilādi
sentences.l: And-of (the) kinds (of) the-perfume and-the-spice, and-of the-aloeswood the-Qāqullī and-the-date the-Indian and-the-olives the-ʿAṣāfīrī, what is-rare its-being-found in these lands.
sentences.i: And of all kinds of perfume and spice, of Qāqullī aloeswood, tamarind and ʿAṣāfīrī olives, things rarely to be found in these lands.”
sentences.n: Again min marks the kinds and mā sums them up. aṣnāf, plural of ṣinf, “kind, sort”. bahār, “spice”, used as a collective. al-ʿūd, “aloeswood”, the fragrant wood burnt as incense; al-qāqullī names the kind by a place, Qāqulla, in the lands of the eastern sea; the vocalisation qāqullī is the likeliest but not certain. al-tamr al-hindī, “the Indian date”, is the tamarind, whence the English name. al-zaytūn al-ʿaṣāfīrī, the olives in which the gold is hidden. nadara, “to be rare”; wujūd, “being found, existence”, is its subject, with -hu for mā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ بِذِكْرِ الزَّيْتُونِ الْعَصَافِيرِىِّ اشْتَهَى قَلْبُهَا ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-malikatu Budūru bi-dhikri al-zaytūni al-ʿaṣāfīriyyi ishtahā qalbuhā dhālika
sentences.l: And-when heard the-queen Budūr of-(the)-mention (of) the-olives the-ʿAṣāfīrī, desired her-heart that.
sentences.i: When Queen Budūr heard ʿAṣāfīrī olives named, her heart longed for them.
sentences.n: samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”: the verb takes bi- for what is heard about; dhikr, “mention”. Here the print spells العصافيرى with final ى, a line after العصافيري with ي; it is the same word, and the shadda is supplied over the ى. ishtahā, Form VIII, “to desire, crave”, often of food.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِصَاحِبِ الْمَرْكَبِ كَمْ مَعَكَ مِنَ الزَّيْتُونِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-ṣāḥibi al-markabi kam maʿaka mina al-zaytūni
sentences.l: And-she-said to-(the)-master (of) the-ship: How-much (is) with-you of the-olives?
sentences.i: And she said to the master of the ship, “How many olives have you?”
sentences.n: li-ṣāḥibi: li- marks the one spoken to; ṣāḥib al-markab, “the master of the ship”, is the captain. kam … min, “how much … of”: min marks what is counted or measured.

sentences.t: قَالَ مَعِي خَمْسُونَ مَطَرًا مَلْآنَةً وَلٰكِنَّ صَاحِبَهَا مَا حَضَرَ مَعَنَا وَالْمَلِكُ يَأْخُذُ مَا اشْتَهَاهُ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: qāla maʿī khamsūna maṭaran malʾānatan wa-lākinna ṣāḥibahā mā ḥaḍara maʿanā wa-al-maliku yaʾkhudhu mā ishtahāhu minhā
sentences.l: He-said: With-me (are) fifty jars full; but their-owner not came with-us, and-the-king takes what he-desires-it of-them.
sentences.i: He said, “I have fifty jars full; but their owner did not come with us, and the king may take whatever he likes of them.”
sentences.n: The print has اشتهاة, a misprint for اشتهاه, corrected here. malʾānatan, “full”, is feminine singular though the counted noun maṭar is masculine: it agrees with the fifty jars as a non-human plural, as -hā does in ṣāḥibahā and minhā; the madda of ملآنة is printed. malʾāna is the feminine of malʾān that the later language uses, where Classical Arabic says malʾā. The print writes lākinna without the long ā, as is usual; it is pointed with a dagger alif. mā ḥaḍara, “did not come”: mā with the perfect is the plain negative of the spoken language. yaʾkhudhu mā ishtahāhu, “takes what he desires”: the imperfect is a courtly “may take”; -hu points back to mā, and the hamza of يأخذ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ أَطْلِعُوهَا فِى الْبَرِّ لِأَنْظُرَ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat aṭliʿūhā fī al-barri li-anẓura ilayhā
sentences.l: And-she-said: Bring-them-up onto the-land, so-that-I-may-look at-them.
sentences.i: She said, “Bring them up on shore, so that I may look at them.”
sentences.n: aṭliʿū, Form IV imperative of ṭalaʿa, “bring up”; -hā is the jars. fī al-barri, “on the land”, as against the sea; the shadda of البرّ is printed and فى is spelt with ى. li-anẓura, “so that I may look”: li- of purpose takes the subjunctive.

sentences.t: فَصَاحَ الرَّئِيسُ عَلَى الْبَحْرِيَّةِ فَطَلَعُوا بِالْخَمْسِينَ مَطَرًا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥa al-raʾīsu ʿalā al-baḥriyyati fa-ṭalaʿū bi-al-khamsīna maṭaran
sentences.l: And-shouted the-captain upon the-sailors, and-they-came-up with-the-fifty jars.
sentences.i: The captain called out to the sailors, and they brought the fifty jars up.
sentences.n: ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to shout at, call to”: ʿalā marks the ones called. al-baḥriyya, “the sailors”, a collective. ṭalaʿa bi-, “to come up with”, that is, “to bring up”: bi- marks what is brought. al-khamsīna maṭaran, “the fifty jars”: the article goes on the number, as the later language has it.

sentences.t: فَفَتَحَتْ وَاحِدًا وَنَظَرَتِ الزَّيْتُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-fataḥat wāḥidan wa-naẓarati al-zaytūna
sentences.l: And-she-opened one and-looked (at) the-olives.
sentences.i: She opened one and looked at the olives,
sentences.n: wāḥidan, “one”, masculine for maṭar. naẓara here takes the olives as a direct object, without ilā, as it often does in the later language.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ أَنَا آخُذُ هٰذِهِ الْخَمْسِينَ مَطَرًا وَأُعْطِيكُمْ حَقَّهَا مَهْمَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat anā ākhudhu hādhihi al-khamsīna maṭaran wa-uʿṭīkum ḥaqqahā mahmā kāna
sentences.l: And-she-said: I take these the-fifty jars and-I-give-you their-due, whatever it-was.
sentences.i: and said, “I will take these fifty jars and pay you their price, whatever it may be.”
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here. anā ākhudhu, “I take”: the imperfect for what one means to do at once; the madda of آخذ is printed. aʿṭā, Form IV, “to give”, takes two objects, -kum, “you”, and ḥaqqahā, “their due”, that is, their price. mahmā kāna, “whatever it was”: after mahmā the perfect has a present or future sense.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الرَّئِيسُ هٰذَا مَالَهُ فِي بِلَادِنَا قِيمَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-raʾīsu hādhā mā lahu fī bilādinā qīmatun
sentences.l: And-said the-captain: This — not to-it in our-lands (is) a-value.
sentences.i: The captain said, “This is worth nothing in our country,
sentences.n: The print sets mā lahu, “there is not to it”, solid as ماله, kept so: mā negates, and li- marks what the value would belong to. qīma, “value, worth”.

sentences.t: وَالَّذِي عَبَّاهَا تَأَخَّرَ عَنَّا وَهُوَ رَجُلٌ فَقِيرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-alladhī ʿabbāhā taʾakhkhara ʿannā wa-huwa rajulun faqīrun
sentences.l: and-the-one-who packed-them stayed-behind from-us, and-he (is) a-man poor.
sentences.i: and the man who packed them stayed behind; he is a poor man.”
sentences.n: ʿabbā, Form II, “to pack”, as above; its shadda is printed. taʾakhkhara ʿan, Form V, “to fall behind, be left behind by”: ʿan marks those he fell behind; the hamza and the shadda of تأخّر are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَمَا مِقْدَارُ ثَمَنِهَا هُنَا فَقَالَ أَلْفُ دِرْهَمٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-mā miqdāru thamanihā hunā fa-qāla alfu dirhamin
sentences.l: And-she-said: And-what (is the) amount (of) their-price here? And-he-said: A-thousand (of) dirham.
sentences.i: She said, “And what is their price here?” He said, “A thousand dirhams.”
sentences.n: wa-mā, “and what”: the wa- picks up the captain's words. miqdār, “measure, amount”; thaman, “price”. alf, “thousand”, takes its noun in the genitive singular: alfu dirhamin. The dirham is the silver coin.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ أَنَا آخُذُهَا بِأَلْفِ دِرْهَمٍ وَأَمَرَتْ بِنَقْلِهَا إِلَى الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: qālat anā ākhudhuhā bi-alfi dirhamin wa-amarat bi-naqlihā ilā al-qaṣri
sentences.l: She-said: I take-them for-a-thousand (of) dirham. And-she-ordered (the) carrying-them to the-palace.
sentences.i: She said, “I will take them for a thousand dirhams,” and gave orders for them to be carried to the palace.
sentences.n: bi-alfi dirhamin, “for a thousand dirhams”: bi- marks the price. The madda of آخذها is printed. amara bi-, “to order”: the verb takes bi- for what is ordered, here naql, “carrying”, with -hā for the jars.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جَاءَ اللَّيْلُ أَمَرَتْ بِإِحْضَارِ مَطَرٍ وَاحِدٍ فَكَشَفَتْهُ وَمَا فِى الْبَيْتِ غَيْرُهَا وَحَيَاةُ النُّفُوسِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jāʾa al-laylu amarat bi-iḥḍāri maṭarin wāḥidin fa-kashafathu wa-mā fī al-bayti ghayruhā wa-Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi
sentences.l: And-when came the-night, she-ordered (the) bringing (of) one jar, and-she-uncovered-it, and-not (was) in the-house other-than-she and-Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.i: When night came she had one jar brought, and uncovered it when there was no one in the room but herself and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs.
sentences.n: amara bi-iḥḍāri, “she ordered the bringing”: bi- again marks what is ordered; iḥḍār is the verbal noun of aḥḍara. kashafa, “to uncover”: the jar's mouth was stopped up. wa-mā fī al-bayti ghayruhā wa-Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi, “and there was none in the house but her and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs”, a circumstantial clause; bayt is here “room, chamber”. Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, “Life of Souls”, is the king's daughter whom Budūr, as king, has married, and who knows her secret; the print spells her name حياة here, as against حيوٰة elsewhere.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَطَّتْ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا طَبَقًا وَقَلَبَتِ الْمَطَرَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaṭṭat bayna yadayhā ṭabaqan wa-qalabati al-maṭara fīhi
sentences.l: Then she-set-down between her-two-hands a-tray, and-turned-over the-jar into-it.
sentences.i: Then she set a tray before her and tipped the jar out into it.
sentences.n: ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, set”, a word much used in the later language; its shadda is printed. bayna yadayhā, “between her hands”, that is, “before her”. ṭabaq, “tray, large platter”. qalaba, “to turn over, upend”: fīhi, “into it”, the tray.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ فِى الطَّبَقِ كَوْمُ ذَهَبٍ أَحْمَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-nazala fī al-ṭabaqi kawmu dhahabin aḥmara
sentences.l: And-came-down into the-tray a-heap (of) gold red.
sentences.i: And down into the tray poured a heap of red gold.
sentences.n: kawm, “heap, pile”, a word of the later language (from the root of kawwama, “to heap up”); the vowel is uncertain, and kūm or kawm may be meant. dhahab aḥmar, “red gold”, pure gold; aḥmar is a diptote, so its genitive ends in -a. فى is spelt with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِلسَّيِّدَةِ حَيَاةِ النُّفُوسِ مَا هٰذَا إِلَّا ذَهَبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat li-al-sayyidati Ḥayāti al-Nufūsi mā hādhā illā dhahaban
sentences.l: And-she-said to-the-lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs: Not (is) this except gold!
sentences.i: She said to the Lady Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, “This is nothing but gold!”
sentences.n: li-al-sayyidati: li- marks the one spoken to; sayyida, “lady”, is the title. mā hādhā illā dhahaban, “this is nothing but gold”: Classical Arabic would say dhahabun, nominative, after mā … illā; the print writes the alif of the accusative, and it is vocalised as printed, a Middle Arabic form. The shadda of الّا is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَحْضَرَتِ الْجَمِيعَ وَاخْتَبَرَتْهَا فَوَجَدَتْهَا كُلَّهَا ذَهَبًا وَالزَّيْتُونُ كُلُّهُ لَمْ يَمْلَأْ مَطَرًا وَاحِدًا
sentences.tr: thumma innahā aḥḍarati al-jamīʿa wa-ikhtabarathā fa-wajadathā kullahā dhahaban wa-al-zaytūnu kulluhu lam yamlaʾ maṭaran wāḥidan
sentences.l: Then indeed-she had-brought the-whole and-tested-them, and-found-them all-of-them gold; and-the-olives, all-of-them, not filled one jar.
sentences.i: Then she had them all brought and tried them, and found them all full of gold: the olives together would not have filled a single jar.
sentences.n: thumma innahā, the narrator's “then”. al-jamīʿ, “the whole”, all the jars. ikhtabara, Form VIII, “to test, try”. wajadathā kullahā dhahaban, “she found them, all of them, gold”: wajada takes two objects, the jars and what they proved to be; kullahā, “all of them”, strengthens -hā. kulluhu, “all of it”, the olives taken together. lam yamlaʾ, “did not fill”: lam with the jussive; the hamza of يملأ is printed.

sentences.t: وَفَتَّشَتْ فِى الذَّهَبِ فَوَجَدَتِ الْفَصَّ فِيهِ فَأَخَذَتْهُ وَتَأَمَّلَتْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-fattashat fī al-dhahabi fa-wajadati al-faṣṣa fīhi fa-akhadhathu wa-taʾammalathu
sentences.l: And-she-searched in the-gold, and-found the-stone in-it, and-took-it and-examined-it.
sentences.i: She searched through the gold and found the stone in it; she took it and looked at it closely,
sentences.n: fattasha fī, Form II, “to search through”: fī marks where the search goes; the shadda of وفتّشت is printed, as is that of الفصّ. al-faṣṣ, “the stone”, the gem Qamar al-Zamān hid in one of the jars. taʾammala, Form V, “to look at closely, consider”; its hamza is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا هُوَ الْفَصُّ الَّذِي كَانَ مَرْبُوطًا عَلَى دِكَّةِ لِبَاسِهَا وَأَخَذَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā huwa al-faṣṣu alladhī kāna marbūṭan ʿalā dikkati libāsihā wa-akhadhahu Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: and-behold, it (was) the-stone which had-been tied upon (the) drawstring (of) her-trousers, and-took-it Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: and behold, it was the very stone that had been tied to the drawstring of her trousers, and that Qamar al-Zamān had taken.
sentences.n: The print has واخذة, a misprint for واخذه, corrected here. wa-idhā huwa, “and behold, it was”: idhā of surprise. marbūṭ ʿalā, “tied onto”, passive participle of rabaṭa: ʿalā marks what it was tied to. dikka, the later language's form of tikka, “the drawstring of trousers”; libās, “clothing”, here the trousers. It was from there that Qamar al-Zamān untied the stone while she slept, the beginning of all their troubles. The shadda of الفصّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَحَقَّقَتْهُ صَاحَتْ مِنْ فَرْحَتِهَا وَخَرَّتْ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taḥaqqaqathu ṣāḥat min farḥatihā wa-kharrat maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And-when she-made-sure-of-it, she-cried-out from her-joy and-fell-down fainted upon-her.
sentences.i: When she was sure of it she cried out for joy and fell to the ground in a swoon.
sentences.n: taḥaqqaqa, Form V, “to make sure of, verify”, here with a direct object. min farḥatihā, “from her joy”: min marks the cause; farḥa, “joy”, a word of the later language beside Classical faraḥ. kharra, “to fall down”; its shadda is printed. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, “fainted upon her”, the stock phrase for “in a swoon”: the passive participle of ghashiya ʿalā, “to come over (someone)”, keeps the ʿalā with its pronoun.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
